SUBJECT:
Conditional Use Permit (CUP No. 25-05/PL No. 25-0400) to convert an existing building to a new
nontraditional college campus in the Urban Neighborhood (UN) zone located at 8500 Long Beach
Boulevard.

PROJECT PROPOSAL/REQUEST:
Request for approval of the adaptive reuse of an existing 11,434-square-foot church building as a
private, nontraditional college campus for a nursing school, including storage for school-related
files and materials. The building is already suitable for use as a nursing school, and only minor
cosmetic improvements are proposed for the interior and exterior.

The request also includes a determination that the project is exempt from the California
Environmental Quality Act (CEQA). Specifically, the project qualifies for a categorical exemption
under CEQA Guidelines Section 15332 (Class 32 – In-Fill Development Projects), as it involves
the adaptive reuse of an existing building located in an urban area and meets all applicable criteria
for a Class 32 exemption.

  Project Location: 8500 Long Beach Boulevard
  Assessor’s Parcel Numbers: 6211-026-016, 6211-026-017
  Property Owners: Eric L. Soto
  Applicant: Andrew Bulaich
  Specific Plan: N/A
  Zoning: Urban Neighborhood (UN)
  District: N/A
  Lot Size: 15,400 square feet (SF), or 0.35 acres (AC)

RECOMMENDATION:

Staff recommends that the Planning Commission:

1. Find that in accordance with CEQA, this project qualifies for a categorical exemption under
  CEQA Guidelines Section 15332, (Class 32) “In-Fill Development Projects”, and is thereby
  exempt from CEQA in that urban uses surround the project site, and the project meets all other
  requirements to qualify for a Class 32 exemption.

2. Adopt Resolution No. 2026-02 approving CUP No. 25-05/PL No. 25-0400 for a new private,
  nontraditional college campus located at 8500 Long Beach Boulevard.

PROJECT DESCRIPTION:
The applicant is proposing to convert an existing religious facility into a private, nontraditional
nursing school that provides remote learning and hands-on lab instruction at the facility for up to
20 students. Per SGMC 11.60.060, the use is considered a “College, Nontraditional Campus,”
defined as follows:

  “College” (land use) means a public or private higher-learning educational facility granting
  degrees, certificates, and academic training, categorized by the following programmatic
  elements:

  2. “Nontraditional campus” means a college in a business/office-oriented setting
  that does not include any form of student housing.

Business Operations

The business operations, use of the building, and support for the project are described as follows:

    Program Scope: This location will operate solely as a Licensed Vocational Nurse (LVN)
  program. Although the company website lists other programs offered system-wide, no
  other programs will be conducted at this satellite campus. This location will function as a
  small satellite campus using a hybrid instructional approach.
    Number of Students: Enrollment will be capped at 20 students per cohort, consistent with
  accreditor requirements. All educational lectures will be delivered remotely, and students
  will only be on site for scheduled, hands-on lab instruction.
    Number of Staff: During on-site instructional periods, the facility will be operated by a
  single educator/staff member.
    Expansion: No future expansion is proposed at this location, and no structural or tenant
  improvements are planned, with the exception of new paint and carpet. The existing
  parking and infrastructure are sufficient for the business.
    Need for School: This project provides an opportunity to address a critical healthcare
  workforce need by preparing students for entry-level nursing roles as an LVN.
    Accreditation: The institution is accredited by the United States Department of Education
  and the Bureau for Private Postsecondary Education.
    Second-Floor Storage – Source of Materials: Items such as books, uniforms, records, and
  instructional supplies serving multiple campuses will be stored on the second floor. Other
  campuses are located in West Covina, Long Beach, Anaheim, Pomona, and Riverside. The
  subject property will function as a centralized support and storage point for the various
  campuses.

    Second-Floor Access & Security: The second floor will be restricted to staff only. Students
  will not be permitted access to the upstairs office and will be formally oriented to the
  building layout. Clear directional and restricted-access signage will be installed to prevent
  unauthorized access.
    Upstairs Office Use: The upstairs office will serve as a touchdown workstation for a
  stockroom clerk. This position is scheduled primarily on weekends and will support
  inventory coordination and material handling.
    Inventory Tracking: The office will be used to track, log, and manage stored materials and
  records associated with our other campuses.
Site Improvements and Project Impacts

The applicant will remove the modular storage container in the parking lot. This will allow
adequate space for the required parking, including providing an ADA-compliant parking stall.
There will be no negative impact to the surrounding area due to the limited scope and staggered
program scheduling. There will also be no negative impact related to traffic, parking, or noise.

The applicant indicates the valuation of site improvements to be $7,000, as this is a reuse of an
existing building and the interior building layout already serves the needs of the school.
Improvements include painting and flooring. According to Public Works, improvements valued at
less than $50,000 are not subject to offsite improvements.

ENVIRONMENTAL ANALYSIS:

Under the California Environmental Quality Act (California Public Resources Code §§ 21000, et
seq., “CEQA”) and the regulations promulgated thereunder (14 California Code of Regulations §§
15000, et seq., the “CEQA Guidelines”), the project qualifies as a Class 32 Categorical Exemption
pursuant to Section 15332 (Class 32 – Infill Development Projects) of the CEQA Guidelines (Title
14, Chapter 3 of the California Code of Regulations).

BACKGROUND:

The institution has been operating for nearly 60 years and has a long-standing track record of
graduating healthcare professionals who serve communities throughout Southern California. The
applicant views this campus as a long-term asset to the City of South Gate and is committed to
contributing to the community through local hiring, community partnerships, and educational
access for the residents of the City.

History and Prior Approvals
The subject property was developed in 1929 with a mortuary. In 1962, a garage was added.
According to business license records, the mortuary operated from 1949 to 1983, when a fire
caused interior damage to the building. On April 17, 1984, the Planning Commission adopted
Resolution No. 84-36, conditionally approving a church site at the subject property.

ANALYSIS:

Required Findings for a CUP: Pursuant to SGMC Section 11.52.030, before a CUP may be
granted, the Planning Commission (or the City Council on appeal) shall make all the following
findings, as applicable to the property:

  A. Approval of the CUP is consistent with and will not adversely affect the intent and purpose
  of this title or the city’s General Plan.

  B. The design and development of the land use and conditions of the CUP are compatible with
  the existing and future land uses of the applicable zone.

  C. Approval of the CUP would not result in detrimental impacts to adjacent properties or to
  the character or function of the neighborhood.

The proposed Resolution supports the findings required under Section 11.52.030.

Development Standards
The proposed project is for the reuse of an existing building and development is not proposed. Site
improvements include painting the interior and exterior of the building and removing an existing
container located in the parking lot.

Issues of Concern

Parking
The site currently has 21 parking spaces. Removal of the container will provide a total of 24 spaces.
Per SGMC Section 11.33.040, Table 11.33-1, trade and/or vocational schools are required to have
a minimum of 3 parking spaces, plus 1 per student capacity. Since the school will serve up to 20
students, a total of 23 parking spaces is required. The project meets this requirement and will be
required to provide one Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA) compliant parking space.

Design/Site Plan Review
No development is proposed since the building is existing. The only site improvements include
painting of the building and additional parking spaces as a result of a container being removed.
There is a requirement under Resolution No. 84-36 to screen any roof-mounted equipment from
street view. However, visibility of the roof-mounted equipment is so minimal that screening would
be more invasive and unnecessary. It is staff’s opinion that the equipment should remain
unscreened.

Landscaping
Landscaping includes some trees and shrubs at the front of the property and along the parking lot.
Removal of the container will provide additional landscape opportunities. A condition has been
added.

   RESOLUTION NO. 2026-02

A RESOLUTION OF THE PLANNING COMMISSION OF THE CITY OF SOUTH GATE,
APPROVING CONDITIONAL USE PERMIT NO. 25-05 (PL NO. 25-0400) TO CONVERT AN
EXISTING BUILDING TO A NEW NONTRADITIONAL COLLEGE CAMPUS, AND OTHER
IMPROVEMENTS LOCATED AT 8500 LONG BEACH BOULEVARD, AND FINDING THE
PROJECT CATEGORICALLY EXEMPT FROM THE CALIFORNIA ENVIRONMENTAL
QUALITY ACT.

  WHEREAS, Andrew Bulaich (“Applicant”), on behalf of World Mission Maranatha Evangelistic
Center Inc. (“Property Owner”), represented by Eric L. Soto, filed a complete application requesting the
approval of a Conditional Use Permit (CUP No. 25-05/PL No. 25-0400) described herein (“Application”);
and

  WHEREAS, the Application pertains to the adaptive reuse of an existing 11,434-square-foot (SF),
two-story religious center building to a nontraditional college campus for a nursing school. The second
floor will be used for storage of school-related files and materials, and minor cosmetic improvements are
proposed for the interior and exterior of the building. The project site consists of approximately 15,400
square feet (0.35 acres) and includes Los Angeles County Assessor’s Parcel Numbers 6211-026-016 and
6211-026-017, commonly known as 8500 Long Beach Boulevard, South Gate, California (the “Property”);
and

  WHEREAS, the Applicant requests approval of CUP No. 25-05 to allow a nontraditional college
campus in the Urban neighborhood (UN) zone. CUP No. 25-05 is subject to the procedures in SGMC
Chapter 11.51 (Permits and Procedures) and Chapter 11.52 (Conditional Use Permit); and

  WHEREAS, Pursuant to South Gate Municipal Code Section 11.52.030, before a CUP may be
granted, the Planning Commission shall make all of the following findings, as applicable to the property:

  (a) Approval of the CUP is consistent with and will not adversely affect the intent and purpose of
  this title or the city’s General Plan.

  (b) The design and development of the land use and conditions of the CUP are compatible with the
  existing and future land uses of the applicable zone.

  (c) Approval of the CUP would not result in detrimental impacts to adjacent properties or to the
  character or function of the neighborhood.

  WHEREAS, notice of the Planning Commission's regular public hearing was published in
compliance with State law in a local newspaper of general circulation on February 5, 2026. In addition, a
public notice was mailed 10 days in advance of the hearing to each property owner, occupant, and resident
within a 1,000-foot radius of the project site, indicating the date and time of the public hearing in accordance
with California Government Code 65091; and

  WHEREAS, on February 17, 2026, the Planning Commission held a regular public hearing to
receive public testimony and other evidence regarding the Application, including without limitation,
information provided to the Planning Commission by City staff and public testimony; and

NOW, THEREFORE, THE PLANNING COMMISSION DOES HEREBY FIND, DETERMINE
AND DECLARE AS FOLLOWS:

SECTION 1.  All of the facts set forth in the recitals are true and correct and are incorporated herein by
reference.

SECTION 2. Based upon substantial evidence presented to this Planning Commission during the public
hearing conducted with regard to the Application, including written staff reports, verbal testimony, site
plans, and Conditions of Approval (“Conditions”) attached hereto as Exhibit “A,” the Planning Commission
hereby specifically finds as follows:

  A. Approval of the CUP is consistent with and will not adversely affect the intent and purpose of this
  title or the city’s General Plan in that Objective CD 2.1, Policy P.1 of the Community Design
  Element encourages the development and redevelopment of areas to “advance a unified and
  coherent pattern of development, maximize the use of land and fill gaps in the urban
  environment.” Objective CD 2.4, Policy P.1 specifies that “the City will seek to expand the
  number and diversity of jobs in the City.” The proposed project is an adaptive reuse of an existing
  underutilized building. The project will bring adult students, teachers, and staff to the college
  campus, creating jobs and providing educational opportunities.

  B. The design and development of the land use and conditions of the CUP are compatible with the
  existing and future land uses of the applicable zone in the Property is located in an urban
  neighborhood area on a major corridor adjacent to commercial uses. The development of a
  college campus will be compatible with the surrounding uses and will encourage pedestrian
  activity.

  A nontraditional college campus will not introduce a new incompatible land use or development
  impacts, as the area is already operating with various activities. The conditions of the CUP will
  ensure that the proposed college campus is appropriately managed, preserving the compatibility

  Sign Theme
  A sign theme or sign program is a coordinated program of one or more signs for an individual commercial
  or industrial business center that can provide an alternative to the general sign regulations. It is intended
  to encourage maximum incentives and latitude in order to achieve variety and good design. Approval
  authority is given to the Planning Commission.

  Sign area and height may not exceed the requirements of the Sign Ordinance unless a sign theme is
  approved by the Planning Commission. Pursuant to SGMC Section 11.36.110.3.b(iii), in reviewing a
  proposed sign theme, the Planning Commission may consider, but is not restricted to, the following
  criteria:

  1.  Are the signs in proportion to the building they serve, i.e., do the height and size of the sign relate
  to the height and size of the building or are the two incompatible?

  2.  The location of the sign on the premises. Is the location of the sign proper, i.e., does a sign or signs
  on surrounding parcels block the view of this sign; does a building or structure interfere with the
  viewing of this sign; do utility poles or lighting poles block the sign; does the location of the sign
  interfere or confuse the readability of traffic control devices (signals)?

  3.  Supportive units to signs shall present an uncluttered appearance.

  4.  Any decision rendered by the city Planning Commission may be appealed to the City Council.
  Such appeal must be submitted in writing to the city clerk no later than ten calendar days after the
  decision was rendered. The City Clerk shall set the matter for hearing, as prescribed by
  Section 11.50.040, Appeals, by the City Council on the earliest convenient date and notify the
  appellant in writing of said date.

  5.  The applicant or his authorized representative should appear in person at the City Council hearing.
  If no such appearance is made by the appellant or his authorized representative, and no continuance
  of said hearing has been requested, the appeal may be denied.

  The proposed sign program provides standards so there is consistency in the appearance of all signs at the
  shopping center. Signs must first be approved by the manager of the shopping center before they are
  presented to the City. The sign program provides direction to new tenants in designing their signs, and
  makes it easier for staff to approve signs based on the standards in the sign program. Consistent signs that
  follow a specific theme have a better appearance and prevent clutter and inconsistencies.

  Pole Signs (Pylon Signs)

  level and the sign face.” A pylon sign is not defined in the Sign Ordinance, but is similar to a pole sign in
  terms of size and height. However, pylon signs often have a wider base, are more decorative, and are more
  visually appealing. Most cities prohibit pole signs in favor of more aesthetically appealing pylon signs.

  the entire shopping center. The second pole sign on Garfield Avenue was approved in 1991 as part of
